L267@P5: As Riguet remarked, difunctional relations generalise both functional relations [16] and pers [17, “quasi-equivalences”]
L268@P5: in the sense that a difunction is characterised by a pair of functional relations whilst a per is characterised by a single

L272@P5: the proofs are quite different, the constructed characterisations are essentially the same, as is made precise in section 4.2.

L18@P0: The notion of a difunction was introduced by Jacques Riguet in 1948. Since then it has
L19@P0: played a prominent role in database theory, type theory, program specification and process
L20@P0: theory. The theory of difunctions is, however, less known in computing than it perhaps
L21@P0: should be. The main purpose of the current paper is to give an account of difunction theory
L22@P0: in relation algebra, with the aim of making the topic more mainstream.
L23@P0: As is common with many important concepts, there are several different but equivalent
L24@P0: characterisations of difunctionality, each with its own strength and practical significance.
L25@P0: This paper compares different proofs of the equivalence of the characterisations.
L26@P0: A well-known property is that a difunction is a set of completely disjoint rectangles. This
L27@P0: property suggests the introduction of the (general) notion of the “core” of a relation;
L28@P0: we use this notion to give a novel and, we believe, illuminating characterisation of
L29@P0: difunctionality as a bijection between the classes of certain partial equivalence relations.

L37@P0: 1. Introduction
L38@P0: This paper is a tribute to our colleague and friend Luís Soares Barbosa, on the occasion of his 60th birthday. Wellversed in the poetic and mathematical discourses, Luís values concise expression, be it in the aesthetic or formal side of his
L39@P0: interests: “beauty is our business”, in the words of Dijkstra [9]. His doctoral research [3] relies on the coalgebra concept [19]
L40@P0: to achieve generality and economy of expression, in particular when combined with the relational algebraic approach [7,6].
L41@P0: Binary relations play a major role in the coalgebraic theory of concurrent processes, which is one of Luís main research
L42@P0: interests. Coalgebras are functions, and as such particular cases of relations; bisimulations are relations, possibly equivalences, as is the case of bisimilarity; and so on and so forth — the list is long.
L43@P0: A concept that unifies many of these situations is that of a difunction. The notion of a difunction was introduced by
L44@P0: Riguet in 1948 [16]. Since then it has played a prominent role in database theory [14]; it also has a significant role, as yet
L45@P0: not fully appreciated, in the development of a theory of types that includes subtyping and types with laws [22].

L52@P1: Difunctions are also used in program specification [13,15] and in the characterisation of certain types of simulations in
L53@P1: process theory [12]. The theory of difunctions is, however, far less known in computing than it should be. The main purpose
L54@P1: of the current paper is to give an account of difunction theory in relation algebra, with the aim of making the topic more
L55@P1: mainstream.
L56@P1: As is common with many important concepts, there are several different but equivalent characterisations of difunctionality, each with its own strength and practical significance. The primary contribution of this paper is to compare different
L57@P1: proofs of the equivalence of the characterisations.
L58@P1: Fig. 1 is a “mental picture” of a difunctional relation of type A∼B. Informally (as first formulated by Riguet [16]), a
L59@P1: difunction is a (heterogeneous) relation that comprises a collection of “completely disjoint rectangles1”.
L60@P1: A special case of a difunction is a partial equivalence relation — “per” for short. Whereas a difunction is pictured as
L61@P1: a collection of completely disjoint rectangles, a per is pictured as a collection of disjoint2 squares, each square of which
L62@P1: pictures an equivalence class.
L63@P1: Like difunctions, there are several different but equivalent characterisations of pers. In the same way that the characterisation of pers as collections of disjoint squares generalises to difunctions as collections of completely disjoint rectangles,
L64@P1: each of the different characterisations of pers generalises to a different characterisation of difunctions. It is well-known, for
L65@P1: example, that a (partial) equivalence relation can be characterised by a (single) functional relation that maps each element
L66@P1: in the domain of the relation to the equivalence class to which it belongs. Similarly —as first formulated by Riguet [16]—
L67@P1: a difunction can be characterised as a pair of functional relations that maps each pair of related elements to the rectangle
L68@P1: to which they belong. The simplest characterisation of a per is, of course, a relation that is symmetric and transitive. (An
L69@P1: equivalence relation is also reflexive.) Symmetry and transitivity can be combined, very concisely, into a single equation;
L70@P1: similarly, the definition of a difunction can be given, also very concisely, as a single equation: see Theorem 25 (in particular
L71@P1: 25(ii)).
L72@P1: In this paper, we assume that the reader has a good understanding of the different characterisations of (partial) equivalence relations outlined above in order to structure our account of the characterisations of difunctions.
L73@P1: Paper structure and summary of contributions To set the scene, the primary contribution of this paper begins in section 3
L74@P1: with a formalisation of a bag/set of “completely disjoint rectangles”; the main result is Theorem 23 which characterises
L75@P1: such a bag/set in terms of a pair of functional relations.
L76@P1: Section 4 is where we prove that —as the name “di”function suggests— a difunctional relation is characterised by a pair
L77@P1: of functional relations. We give two quite different constructions in subsection 4.3, which are shown to be isomorphic.
L78@P1: The steps taken in the generalisation of properties of pers to properties of difunctions can be taken yet further: we
L79@P1: introduce the (general) notion of the “core” of an arbitrary relation; in section 5, we use this notion to give a novel and,
L80@P1: we believe, illuminating characterisation of difunctionality as a bijection between the classes of certain partial equivalence
L81@P1: relations.
L82@P1: Before we can begin on this endeavour, it is necessary to summarise the axiom system that we call “relation algebra”
L83@P1: (section 2). Central to our relational reasoning are the left and right “domains” of a relation, of which there are two kinds:
L84@P1: coreflexive domains and per domains, both playing a vital role in what follows. Section 6 discusses the relative merits of the
L85@P1: proofs we have presented, in particular with respect to our limited use of points and entirely point-free calculations. We
L86@P1: also briefly mention ongoing work on “cores” and “indexes” of a relation.
